solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Labour leader welcomed by social class in eg Leeds

indicators.note: whoever is welcomed is taken inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a caste is a hereditary social class

indicators.note: a leader goes at the front, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A Labour politician is received by the local social elite in a northern city.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds looks like the city in Yorkshire, but here it is Leeds Castle in Kent; CASTE takes in the L to make CASTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeds Castle is a famous moated fortress in Kent, so it serves as an example of the answer.

clue.text: Firm about an offence where bets are placed

indicators.note: one thing about another goes around it, so the outer piece wraps the inner

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
the indefinite article
a sin is a moral offence

explanation.surface: A company is caught up in some wrongdoing at a betting venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm about' reads as 'firm on the subject of'; here the firm's two letters sit on either side of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A casino is a building for gambling, where people stake money on games of chance.

clue.text: It gives information about family certain to go round Vietnam briefly

indicators.note: to put it briefly is to shorten it, so part of the word is dropped
going round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: sure means certain
'Nam is the familiar short form of the country's name

explanation.surface: Someone researching family history is sure to go round Vietnam.
explanation.walkthrough: The inserted piece does not land in the middle of its host but after its second letter, which is the part solvers tend to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A surname is the family name, so it tells you which family a person belongs to.

clue.text: Policy of alliance oddly abandoned

indicators.note: if the odd-numbered letters are abandoned, only the even-numbered ones remain

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A party's stance on alliances has been bizarrely dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' sounds like 'strangely', but it means the odd letters, and 'abandoned' says those go.
explanation.definitionFit: A party line is its official policy or position, the stance members are expected to take.

clue.text: Prominently publicise cut restricting parking

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one piece is held within the other

parts.note: to slash is to cut
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A newspaper trumpets a cut in the parking available.
explanation.walkthrough: SLASH holds P after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers splash a story when they print it big across the front page, giving it maximum prominence.

clue.text: Host anti-monarchy guy abandoning Religious Education

indicators.note: whatever is abandoned is left behind, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: a republican opposes rule by a monarch
RE is the school subject abbreviation

explanation.surface: A man who opposes the monarchy walks out of a religion class.
explanation.walkthrough: REPUBLICAN loses its opening RE to leave PUBLICAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A publican runs a pub and is known as the landlord or host to drinkers there.

clue.text: Performer in plant ignoring outsiders

indicators.note: outsiders are the letters on the outside, and ignoring them removes the first and last

parts.note: a plant is an industrial works

explanation.surface: An entertainer working in a factory keeps clear of strangers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' suggests something growing, but it is the industrial kind; FACTORY without F and Y gives ACTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor performs roles on stage or screen, so is one kind of performer.

clue.text: One offered to help with the Spanish for composer

parts.note: a hand is a helper, as when someone offers to lend a hand
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A volunteer assists some Spanish people in finding a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the two parts: HAND + EL.
explanation.definitionFit: George Frideric Handel wrote Messiah and the Water Music, a famous Baroque composer.

clue.text: Unusual garnets recollected

indicators.note: re-collected means gathered up again, so the letters are put back together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone remembers some unusual gemstones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recollected' reads as remembered; split it as re-collected and it is a gathering again of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange and unusual are straightforward synonyms, both meaning odd or out of the ordinary.

clue.text: Basic telex with edges missing occupying the mind

indicators.note: the edges of a word are its outer letters, and missing means they are gone

parts.note: the word without its outer letters
mental means relating to the mind

explanation.surface: A simple message sent by telex, its edges torn, preoccupies someone.
explanation.walkthrough: TELEX loses T and X, then MENTAL follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemental describes something fundamental or primary, the most basic level of a thing.

clue.text: Exhortation to continue at crease getting stick?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: split into two words, an urging to a cricketer to keep batting
second meaning: a short rod, as used by a conductor or relay runner

explanation.surface: A batsman is urged to keep going while being heckled.
explanation.walkthrough: The crease is the line a cricket batsman stands at; 'bat on!' tells them to keep batting. Run together, the two words make a single noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A baton is a short thin rod, carried by conductors, police officers and relay runners.

clue.text: Orderly scene a teacher takes in

indicators.note: to take something in is to contain it, so the letters sit inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A teacher surveys a calm, well-ordered classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle sceNE A Teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat and orderly both describe something tidy, arranged with everything in its place.

clue.text: Pie demolished with greed? It runs in the family!

indicators.note: something demolished is knocked to pieces, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wolfs a pie greedily, a trait apparently inherited from their relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that gluttony runs in the family; the definition works on its own too.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedigree is a line of ancestry, a record of descent passed down through generations.

clue.text: Using force, get rid of nonsense over female deer, reportedly

parts.note: bull is slang for nonsense

indicators.note: a report is something told, so the word is taken as it is spoken

parts.note: does are female deer

explanation.surface: Someone forcibly clears away rubbish lying over a doe, or so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the first piece above the second: BULL then DOZE.
explanation.definitionFit: To bulldoze is to flatten or clear away by brute force, like the earth-moving machine.

clue.text: Untax beer? That could make you full of vitality!

indicators.note: what the letters could make is something else built from them, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Scrapping the duty on beer would put drinkers in high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a campaign slogan; the nine letters of the first two words are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Exuberant means lively and energetic, bursting with high spirits and enthusiasm.

clue.text: Track crossing Virginia, hard work

indicators.note: a path crossing a region runs through it, so one piece lies across the other

parts.note: a trail is a track
VA is the postal abbreviation for the US state

explanation.surface: A route across Virginia takes a lot of effort to walk.
explanation.walkthrough: US states are regularly clued by their two-letter postal codes.
explanation.definitionFit: Travail is an old word for painful or laborious effort, toil that tires you out.

clue.text: Runner of errands accommodating learner — one on course?

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room, so one piece is housed inside the other

parts.note: a gofer is a dogsbody who runs errands
L is the learner-driver plate

explanation.surface: An errand boy takes in a trainee to keep them on track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On course' suggests being on schedule, but the course is a golf course; the question mark flags that.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer plays on a golf course, so someone found on the links fits the cryptic hint.

clue.text: Aid for snooker player as pride's shattered

indicators.note: anything shattered breaks into bits, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written, with the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A snooker player needs help after a humiliating defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored, so the fodder is the six letters of PRIDES.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider is a raised cue rest with long legs that lets a snooker player reach over other balls.

clue.text: Old Boy, by himself, note, unfashionable

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for a former pupil of a school
sole means alone
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A lonely former pupil writes a note about being out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: OB + SOLE + TE, three pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsolete means out of date and no longer in use, so it is outmoded or passé.

clue.text: Alarm mechanism in premises I rented

indicators.note: something in a phrase is contained within it, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A burglar alarm is fitted in a flat someone has leased.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle premiseS I RENted.
explanation.definitionFit: A siren is a device making a loud wailing noise to warn of danger, such as an emergency.

clue.text: Hire purchase securing a rookie's first musical instrument

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece is gripped inside the other

parts.note: the initial letters of the two words; hire purchase is the British term for buying on instalments
taken as written

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A beginner buys their first instrument on the instalment plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hire purchase' is the British term for buying on credit and paying in instalments; it wraps A and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A harp is a large stringed instrument plucked with the fingers, one kind of instrument.

clue.text: Initially missed out, angry newbies complain

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives up its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Beginners who were left out at first are cross and grumble about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially missed out' reads as a phrase, but 'Initially' applies to each of the next four words.
explanation.definitionFit: To moan is to grumble or whine, an informal synonym for complaining about something.

clue.text: Give up supporting attempt

parts.note: to be for something is to support it
a go is a try

explanation.surface: Someone abandons their backing for an effort.
explanation.walkthrough: FOR + GO.
explanation.definitionFit: To forgo is to do without or relinquish something, to surrender a claim to it.

clue.text: English musical work cornered by fat cat

indicators.note: what is cornered is hemmed in on all sides, so one piece is trapped inside another

parts.note: lard is pig fat
E is the abbreviation for English
op. is short for opus, a numbered composition

explanation.surface: An English composition is trapped by an overweight cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat cat' reads as a wealthy person; split it, and fat is LARD while cat is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A leopard is a large spotted wild feline of Africa and Asia, one of the big cats.

clue.text: Heard songbird in French city

indicators.note: what is heard is taken in by the ear, so the spoken form counts, not the spelling

parts.note: a wren is a tiny songbird

explanation.surface: Someone hears a bird singing in a French town.
explanation.walkthrough: The French city name is pronounced like the bird, with its double N and final ES silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Rennes is the capital of Brittany in north-western France, a major regional city.

clue.text: Rage about heel, ultimately scheming type

indicators.note: one thing about another goes around it, so the outer piece wraps the inner

parts.note: anger is rage

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Fury at a cad who turns out to be a schemer.
explanation.walkthrough: A heel is a cad, which suits the surface, but here only its last letter counts; ANGER goes round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who angles for something manoeuvres slyly to get it, so an angler here is a schemer.
